Imagine walking along the edge
of a quiet pond on a warm summer afternoon.
Dragonflies drift through the reeds,
crickets call from the grass,
and the water lies perfectly still.
It looks like a picture of untouched nature.
But beneath that calm surface,
something strange can happen to the frogs.
A creature too small to see without
a microscope can change the way
a tadpole's body is built,
and the result can be a frog
with legs where no legs should be.
Our story begins on August 8,
1995, in southern Minnesota.
A group of students from the
Minnesota New Country School were
exploring a pond in the Ney Wildlife
Preserve, near the small town of Henderson.
They were catching northern leopard
frogs, an ordinary sight in the Midwest.
But the frogs they pulled from
the water were not ordinary.
Some had missing legs.
Some had twisted legs.
And some had extra legs.
The students counted eleven deformed
frogs and told their teacher.
Their teacher called the Minnesota
Pollution Control Agency.
A research scientist named Judy
Helgen took the call.
Within days, her team was wading
into the same pond.
What they found was worse than
the students had described.
Frogs with legs that did not work.
Frogs with legs bent at impossible angles.
Frogs missing an eye.
This was not one unlucky animal.
Something seemed to be going wrong
for a large part of the whole population.
Here are the numbers from that pond.
On August 18, 1995,
60 percent of the 53 frogs collected
were deformed.
A week later, the team collected
137 frogs, and 76 percent were deformed.
And in September 1996,
47 percent of 70 frogs were deformed.
The story spread fast.
Newspapers and television picked
it up, and people across Minnesota
began calling in their own sightings.
By the end of September 1996,
reports had come from 55 of the
state's 87 counties, at 172 locations.
Soon, deformed frogs were being
reported in other states and in
southern Canada too.
And people began asking a
frightening question.
If something in the water was doing
this to frogs, what might it be
doing to the people who lived nearby?
There was a good reason to worry.
Frogs are often called living alarm systems.
Their skin is thin,
and it takes in water and air
directly from their surroundings.
They also spend their early lives
in water, as tadpoles,
before moving onto land.
So whatever is in a pond can
reach a frog quickly.
If frogs were suddenly growing
extra legs, it seemed natural to
suspect that something toxic had
entered the water.
What else could build a frog so wrong?
In September 1996, scientists met
in Duluth to compare ideas.
Some suspected pesticides.
Others suspected stronger
ultraviolet light, reaching the
ground through a thinning ozone layer.
Another researcher showed that
a chemical called retinoic acid
could trigger extra limbs in the
lab, and he pointed out that a
common insecticide, methoprene,
was related to it.
Each idea pointed toward the same
uncomfortable conclusion: that
modern human chemicals were changing
the bodies of wild animals.
But one scientist at that meeting
had a very different idea.
Stan Sessions, a biologist from
New York, argued that the culprit
might not be a chemical at all.
He suggested a parasite.
If certain parasites infected
tadpoles while their legs were
first forming, he said,
they could cause extra limbs.
Sessions had first proposed this
idea years earlier, in 1987.
At the time, few people paid much attention.
The chemical explanations simply
seemed more likely.
Far away in California,
a Stanford University student named
Pieter Johnson had been following the story.
In December 1996, he began a project
of his own.
Instead of starting with chemicals,
he went out to ponds in Santa
Clara County, south of San
Francisco, where Pacific treefrogs
were turning up with deformed legs.
He looked closely at what lived
in those ponds.
And he noticed something interesting.
The ponds with deformed frogs also
had a particular kind of snail.
When Johnson and his colleagues
examined the deformed frogs,
they found tiny cysts packed around
the base of the hind legs.
Inside each cyst was a young
flatworm, a parasite called
Ribeiroia ondatrae.
Its name has a strange history.
The species was first described
in 1931 from worms found in the
livers of muskrats, and muskrats
belong to the genus Ondatra.
A parasite named after a muskrat
was now the prime suspect in the
mystery of the monster frogs.
But finding a parasite inside a
deformed frog does not prove that
the parasite caused the deformity.
So Johnson ran an experiment.
His team took Pacific treefrog
eggs from ponds with no parasites
and raised the tadpoles in tanks.
Some tanks received Ribeiroia,
at levels similar to the wild ponds.
The others did not.
The results were striking.
In the parasite tanks,
deformities appeared in 85 percent
of the frogs.
The tadpoles raised without the
parasite developed normally.
The findings were published in
the journal Science in April 1999,
less than a year after Johnson graduated.
In the same issue,
Stan Sessions and his colleagues
reported on frogs from twelve
locations in California, Oregon,
Arizona, and New York.
They found many limbs that were
mirror images of each other,
a pattern typical of parasite infection.
For the first time,
there was strong evidence that
a natural parasite could build
these monster frogs.
So was the Minnesota mystery solved?
Not exactly.
The parasite clearly explained
deformed frogs in many western ponds.
But in Minnesota, the investigation
never reached a firm answer.
The state agency ended its study
in 2001, citing budget limits.
To this day, the cause of the
Minnesota frogs is considered
inconclusive, and many scientists
think more than one cause may have
been involved.
No one knows for sure what happened
in that pond in 1995.
To understand how a tiny worm can
do this, we need to follow its life.
Ribeiroia ondatrae cannot complete
its life inside a single animal.
It needs three different hosts.
First, a snail.
Second, a tadpole or a small fish.
And finally, a bird or a mammal,
such as a heron,
a hawk, a duck,
or even a badger.
The journey begins at the bottom
of the pond, inside a snail with
a coiled, flat shell:
the ram's horn snail.
It starts with a tiny swimming
larva called a miracidium,
which hatches from an egg in the water.
When it finds a ram's horn snail,
it gets inside.
There, the parasite multiplies,
making many copies of itself without mating.
And as these young parasites feed,
they eat the snail's reproductive tissue.
The snail is castrated.
It can no longer produce young of its own.
Instead, its body becomes a factory,
working for the parasite.
Inside the snail, the parasite
produces a new stage called cercariae.
These are free-swimming larvae
with a tail, shaped a little like
tiny tadpoles themselves.
And there can be a lot of them.
Researchers have reported that
a single infected snail can release
more than 1,000 cercariae in one night.
Like the cercariae of other flukes,
they do not feed.
They have only a short time to
find their next target:
a growing tadpole.
Picture a tadpole swimming in the
warm shallows.
At this stage, its body is changing fast.
Near the base of its tail,
small clusters of cells called
limb buds are starting to form.
These buds will become its back legs.
Each one holds the instructions
to build a thigh,
a knee, an ankle,
a foot, and toes,
all in the right order.
And it is exactly here,
around these young limb buds,
that the cercariae tend to gather.
The cercariae burrow through the
tadpole's thin skin and leave their
swimming tails behind.
Once inside, each one wraps itself
in a protective wall and becomes
a cyst, a resting stage called a metacercaria.
In infected tadpoles, large numbers
of these cysts build up near the
base of the hind legs.
And it does not take many.
Researchers have reported that
as few as 12 cercariae can kill
or deform a single tadpole.
So how does a cyst make a
leg grow twice?
Scientists are still working that out.
One idea is mechanical.
The cysts may physically push apart
the cells of the growing limb bud,
splitting one set of instructions
into several.
Earlier lab experiments supported this idea.
Researchers implanted tiny inert
beads into the developing limb
buds of salamanders and frogs,
and extra limb structures grew.
If plain beads can do it,
a cyst sitting in the same place
might do it too.
The other idea is chemical.
Limbs are guided by signaling
molecules, and one of the most
important is retinoic acid,
a substance made from vitamin A.
In 2012, a team of researchers
measured it in wood frog tadpoles.
Limb buds with Ribeiroia inside
had about 70 percent more retinoic
acid than limb buds without the parasite.
That does not prove the whole story.
But it suggests the parasite may
be scrambling the chemical
instructions that tell a limb how to grow.
When those instructions break down,
the results can be extraordinary.
An infected limb bud can produce
two or three legs instead of one,
and each extra leg is often a
mirror image of its neighbor.
According to Johnson's lab,
the parasite has been shown to
cause up to six extra limbs,
for a total of ten legs on
a single frog.
The extra legs usually grow from
the hips, because that is where
the cysts gather.
But extra legs are only part of the picture.
The parasite can also cause the opposite.
Some frogs end up with legs that
are partly or completely missing.
Others have skin webbing that binds
a leg against the body,
bony bridges that lock a joint
in place, or extra or missing toes.
Hind legs are hit most often.
And researchers report that in
some populations, these
malformations can affect more than
half of the young frogs leaving a pond.
Now imagine being one of those frogs.
A healthy frog depends on strong,
well-timed back legs.
It uses them to leap away from
danger, dive into the water,
and snap up fast insects.
A frog with extra legs dangling
from its hips, or with legs bound
by skin, cannot do these things well.
Every jump becomes clumsy.
Every escape becomes slower.
But how much slower?
In 2011, two researchers decided
to measure it.
Brett Goodman and Pieter Johnson
compared malformed frogs with normal ones.
The malformed frogs jumped 41
percent shorter distances.
They swam 37 percent slower.
And they caught 55 percent fewer crickets.
On every test that mattered for
survival, the deformed frogs fell far behind.
Out in real ponds,
the results were grim.
In ordinary ponds, more than a
fifth of the parasitized frogs
died every two weeks,
and almost no deformed frogs were
left among the adults.
Malformed frogs rarely live long
enough to breed.
And the parasite can kill outright, too.
In lab studies, even low levels
of infection caused 30 to 95 percent
mortality in some frogs and toads.
For a tadpole, Ribeiroia is far
more than a strange curiosity.
This raises a puzzling question.
Why would a parasite damage the
animal it lives in?
Many parasites do best when their
hosts stay alive for a long time.
A deformed frog that cannot hop
seems like a terrible home.
So what could the parasite possibly gain?
To find a possible answer,
we have to look at where its
life cycle ends.
Not in the pond.
Not in the frog.
But in the sky above the water.
Look up from the pond.
A great blue heron stands in the
shallows, perfectly still, watching.
Herons, ducks, and hawks are among
the final hosts of Ribeiroia.
Only inside a bird or a mammal
can the parasite grow into an adult
and reproduce.
But a cyst hidden in a tadpole's
hip cannot fly.
To reach the bird,
the frog carrying it has to be eaten.
And this is where the deformities
may play a role.
Scientists have proposed that the
deformities may help the parasite.
A healthy frog can spot a hunting
heron and leap into deep water.
A frog with tangled extra legs
is much easier to catch.
If deformed frogs are eaten more
often, more parasites reach the
birds they need.
Interestingly, Goodman and Johnson
found that in a pond with no
predators, extra legs had no
significant effect on survival.
That fits the idea:
the danger of deformity comes mostly
from being hunted.
When a bird swallows an infected
frog, the cysts are freed in its gut.
The young worms move along the
intestine and attach to its lining.
There, well fed, they grow into
adults and begin producing eggs.
Those eggs leave the bird in its droppings.
And because birds travel,
they can carry the parasite to
new ponds and wetlands,
sometimes far from where the infection began.
In about two to three weeks,
the eggs in the water are ready
to hatch, and the cycle starts again.
Was this parasite something new
in the 1990s?
Not at all.
Some reports of malformed amphibians
go back more than two hundred years.
In 2003, Pieter Johnson and his
colleagues looked through records
from 1946 to 1988.
They found nine historical hot
spots in seven states,
and at most of them they found
signs of the parasite in preserved specimens.
Ribeiroia had been building extra
legs on frogs long before the
students in Minnesota ever dipped their nets.
But something had changed.
When the team revisited three of
the old sites, they still found
the parasite, and severe
malformations in 7 to 50 percent
of the frogs.
Before 1990, fewer than a dozen
such sites were known.
In the years that followed,
more than 50 new hot spots were found.
And at Jette Pond in Montana,
malformations in Pacific treefrogs
rose from about 20 percent in 1960
to about 46 percent in 2000.
Why would an old parasite suddenly
become so common?
The answer may lead back to us after all.
Farms, lawns, and cattle pastures
release nitrogen and phosphorus,
the nutrients found in fertilizer and manure.
When rain washes these nutrients
into ponds, it changes the whole food web.
Algae grow faster.
And ram's horn snails,
which graze on algae,
have more to eat.
More snails can mean more homes for Ribeiroia.
In 2007, Johnson and his colleagues
reported a test of whether this
chain reaction really happens.
They built 36 outdoor ponds and
added nutrients to some of them.
In the enriched ponds,
the total mass of snails rose by
nearly 50 percent.
Infected snails there released
about twice as many cercariae.
And tadpoles in the enriched ponds
carried two to five times more infection.
Johnson described it as watching
nutrient pollution move through
the parasite's life cycle as it
cascaded through the food web.
It is a remarkable chain.
Fertilizer feeds algae.
Algae feed snails.
Snails feed parasites.
And parasites, in turn, reshape frogs.
Other chemicals may add to the problem.
The herbicide atrazine, for example,
has been reported to weaken
amphibian immune systems, which
could make frogs more vulnerable to infection.
There is a hopeful twist, though.
In 2013, Johnson's team published
a huge survey: 345 wetlands in
California, more than 24,000
amphibians examined, and more than
17,000 snails dissected.
Ponds with more kinds of amphibians
had far fewer deformed frogs,
about 78.5 percent fewer than ponds
with few species.
The parasite did best in Pacific treefrogs.
One explanation is that when other
species share the pond,
many parasites end up in hosts
where they do less harm.
Could a richer pond really protect frogs?
The team tested the idea in the lab.
When the parasite was added to
tanks holding tadpoles of several
species, the animals carried about
half as many parasites as in tanks
with a single species.
In a related study,
toad tadpoles raised alongside
gray treefrogs had 37 percent less
infection and fewer malformations.
In other words, a pond full of
different neighbors can work a
little like a shield.
All of this matters because
amphibians are already in trouble.
A global assessment of more than
6,000 amphibian species found that
32 percent were threatened and
43 percent were declining.
Habitat loss and a deadly fungal
disease called chytrid have hit
many species hard.
Parasite deformities are only one
part of that picture.
But in ponds where they are common,
they remove young frogs before
they can grow up and breed,
adding one more pressure to animals
already under strain.
The story of the monster frogs
teaches a powerful lesson.
At first, it looked like a simple
case of poison in the water.
In the end, it involved farmers
and fertilizer, algae and snails,
flatworms and tadpoles, herons and hawks.
Even the number of frog species
in a pond played a part.
When we change one strand of
nature's web, the effect can travel
through every other strand,
in ways that are very hard to predict.
It is easy to see Ribeiroia as
a horror story, and in a way it is.
But it is also a remarkable piece
of evolution.
Without eyes and without a brain,
this tiny flatworm moves through
snails, tadpoles, and birds,
and along the way it can reshape
the body of a vertebrate.
Nature does not judge whether that
is cruel or clever.
It only keeps what works.
And for this parasite,
the strategy has worked for a very long time.
So the next time you stand beside
a quiet pond, look a little closer.
Under that still surface,
snails graze, tadpoles grow,
and invisible parasites search
for their next host.
Most frogs you see will be perfectly normal.
But each one has survived a world
we are only beginning to understand.
If this story changed how you see
a simple pond, subscribe to Miya's
Lab, and let's keep looking beneath
the surface together.
Thanks for watching.
